reference_title: EM 1110-2-2107, Design of Hydraulic Steel Structures (USACE, dated 1 August 2022)

sections.title: Design for Fatigue
sections.summary: All cyclically loaded HSS must be designed for fatigue using AISC 360 or AASHTO stress-life procedures (finite vs. infinite/indefinite life, Figure 5.1's S-N curves); selecting AISC/AASHTO detail categories (A-C preferred, D-E avoided); the stress-range screening rule (net-tension-only, factor of safety 2.0 against the live-load tensile stress exceeding half the dead-load compressive stress); stress determination methods (simplified Chapter 9/10 models or instrumentation); the annual-maximum stress-cycle magnitude convention (or Miner's Rule for statistical loading); number-of-cycles selection; and distortion-induced fatigue.
sections.body: All cyclically loaded HSS must be designed for the fatigue limit state. The stress-life procedures defined in AISC 360 and AASHTO must be used (either is acceptable); two fatigue stress limits are considered -- finite life and infinite life (called 'indefinite life' in AISC 360, the same concept) -- represented by the S-N (Stress Range-Number of Stress Cycles) curves of Figure 5.1 (sloping curves = finite life, horizontal curve = infinite life). Finite life implies fatigue damage will occur under a given stress-range/cycle-count combination; a design is acceptable when the combined stress range and cycle count exceed the selected detail category's fatigue strength, so a load factor of 1.0 is applied to loads used to compute fatigue stress for this check (Table 4.1 footnote 5; infinite life uses 2.0 for all loads). Details should be selected so fatigue cracking will not occur over the structure's life: the AISC/AASHTO detail category matching the connection detail's geometry/configuration/stress-concentration degree governs the design limit state; Categories A-C are generally preferred, Categories D-E should be avoided where possible. Where fatigue is governed by weld-toe cracking, resistance can be improved via post-weld toe treatments (ultrasonic impact treatment, heat treatment, grinding, GTAW/plasma remelting, hammer/shot peening). Stress ranges are calculated for LIVE LOAD stresses only, as the difference between minimum and maximum values over one cycle (compression and tension within one cycle are summed as absolute values). Details are fatigue-prone only under net TENSION stress: if the live-load tensile stress is less than half the simultaneously-occurring dead-load compressive stress, a fatigue check is not required (an implied factor of safety of 2.0). Stresses are determined via appropriate analysis (load path/distribution/boundary conditions); the simplified load models of Chapters 9-10 may suffice, or instrumentation of similar HSS combined with refined analysis. The assumed stress magnitude per cycle is the average annual maximum stress (e.g. from the hydrostatic head at a 1-year return period), applied for the design-life cycle count; alternatively, the statistical loading variation can be used with Miner's Rule (or another averaging technique) for an equivalent fatigue loading. The number of stress cycles must be based on the selected stress range and must consider multiple stress ranges occurring during a load cycle. Distortion-induced fatigue (from out-of-plane forces) must be addressed via proper detailing or fatigue design using refined-analysis stresses and a detail category based on the connection's assumed resistance.
key_points: AISC 360 or AASHTO stress-life procedure, either acceptable
Finite-life fatigue load factor = 1.0; infinite-life = 2.0, all loads (fatigue_fracture.fatigue_load_factor)
Detail categories A-C preferred; D-E avoided where possible
Fatigue screening: no check needed if live-load tension < 0.5x simultaneous dead-load compression (fatigue_fracture.fatigue_check_required)
Stress magnitude convention: average annual maximum stress (e.g. 1-yr return-period hydrostatic head), or Miner's Rule for statistical loading
sections.applicability: Determining whether a detail needs a fatigue check at all, and if so, which stress-life procedure and detail category govern.

sections.title: Design for Fracture
sections.summary: The fracture limit state prevents brittle fracture via minimized stress concentration/constraint and proper material properties; Fracture Critical Member (FCM) determination via redundancy analysis (a member may avoid FCM status if refined analysis shows adequate post-fracture strength/stability, using load factor 1.0, resistance factor 1.0, and a 90%-of-yield stress cap); the Fracture Control Plan (per AASHTO/AWS, or an Engineer-established plan using fracture mechanics); and constraint avoidance at connections. Fracture mechanics (Fitness for Service) is an alternative path per EM 1110-2-6054.
sections.body: The fracture limit state must be considered to prevent brittle fracture: design must minimize stress concentrations, minimize constraint, and specify proper material properties; stress concentrations are controlled through detailing/fabrication specifications, following fatigue-design detailing practices. The Engineer identifies all FCM present in the design, using any rational engineering analysis that adequately represents load redistribution from the analyzed member, evaluating all applicable load combinations. For the strength limit state in this redundancy analysis, all applicable load combinations are evaluated with a load factor of 1.0 on every load and a resistance factor of 1.0 on the applicable strength limit -- but in no case may the resulting stress exceed 90 percent of yield (fatigue_fracture.fracture_critical_redundancy_check). The serviceability limit state is evaluated separately where the HSS must function after damage. If refined analysis demonstrates adequate strength/stability to avoid partial or total collapse with a member assumed fractured (via redistribution or redundancy), that member may be considered redundant and NOT determined an FCM (see AASHTO's Guide Specifications for Analysis and Identification of Fracture Critical Members and System Redundant Members); refined analyses using plastic redistribution, plastic mechanisms, large-displacement theory, or other advanced techniques require CECW-CE approval. FCM/components must be designed/fabricated per the AASHTO/AWS Fracture Control Plan (FCP, see Chapter 8), or the Engineer may establish an FCP using fracture mechanics as a basis, including hydrogen control and other welding controls limiting cracking potential. Constraint must be avoided at all connections through proper detailing/fabrication unless it can be shown that a connection failure will not adversely affect overall safety/performance. In lieu of this chapter's guidance, the fracture limit state can instead be addressed directly through fracture mechanics per EM 1110-2-6054's Fitness for Service (FFS) procedure.
key_points: FCM redundancy check: gamma=1.0, phi=1.0, stress capped at 0.90*Fy (fatigue_fracture.fracture_critical_redundancy_check)
A member need not be treated as FCM if refined analysis shows the structure survives its fracture (redistribution/redundancy)
FCM/components follow the AASHTO/AWS Fracture Control Plan, or an Engineer-established fracture-mechanics-based FCP
Advanced redundancy analyses (plastic redistribution, large-displacement theory, etc.) require CECW-CE approval
Alternative path: full fracture-mechanics Fitness for Service per EM 1110-2-6054
sections.applicability: Determining whether a member must be treated as fracture-critical, and the associated fabrication/QC requirements if so.
